analysis.one_liner: Bans new federal offshore oil and gas leasing next to coastal states that have banned drilling in their own waters.
analysis.headline: The bill, backed by 15 Senate Democrats, never got a hearing or vote in the Energy and Natural Resources Committee before the 104th Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would amend the Outer Continental Shelf Lands Act to bar the Interior Department from issuing new oil and gas leases on federal submerged lands off the coast of any state that has declared a moratorium on drilling in its own waters. It was referred to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee and never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the 104th Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Residents of coastal states with drilling moratoria, whose beaches, fisheries, and coastal economies would be shielded from new offshore oil and gas leasing just off their shores; coastal fishing and tourism businesses that depend on unpolluted waters.

how_it_helps.text: Gives a coastal state's drilling ban real force by extending it to adjacent federal waters, which the Interior Department could otherwise lease over the state's objection.
Protects the beaches, fisheries, and tourism economies of moratorium states from new offshore exploration and production next door.

analysis.who_pays: Offshore oil and gas companies, which could no longer obtain new federal leases in waters adjacent to states with moratoria, and the federal government, which would forgo lease revenue from those areas.

drawbacks.text: Blocking leases off moratorium states would reduce domestic oil and gas production and the federal lease revenue that comes from the Outer Continental Shelf, at a time when opponents argued the country needed energy supply.

The bill effectively hands governors a veto over federal submerged lands beyond state jurisdiction, which critics saw as a state takeover of federally owned resources held in trust for the whole nation.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offered a clear benefit — coastal states could make their drilling bans stick against federal leases just offshore — at the cost of foregone federal energy leasing and revenue in those waters. The main design criticism is that it delegates sweeping control over federal waters to individual governors; whether that is a feature or a flaw depends on how much weight one gives coastal states' say over their own shorelines. The bill never got enough consideration for those tradeoffs to be debated on the record.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee the day it was introduced, and the committee never acted on it, so it died when the 104th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Barbara Boxer introduced the bill on June 20, 1995, joined by 14 Democratic cosponsors at introduction.

The bill's single substantive provision would prohibit the Interior Secretary from leasing Outer Continental Shelf lands seaward of or adjacent to any coastal state with a statutory or governor-ordered moratorium on drilling.
The Senate read the bill twice and referred it to the Energy and Natural Resources Committee the same day.
No further action — no hearing, markup, or floor vote — appears in the record before the 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Offshore oil and gas interests, which faced no new statutory restrictions on leasing federal waters next to moratorium states, and any federal leasing plans that proceeded without those limits.

for.name: Barbara Boxer
for.role: U.S. Senator from California, bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to bar federal offshore leasing next to states with drilling moratoria.

against.name: Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee
against.role: Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee
against.what_they_did: Held the bill after referral and took no action on it for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Frank Murkowski
against.role: Chair, Senate Energy and Natural Resources Committee
against.what_they_did: As committee chair in the 104th Congress, never scheduled the bill for consideration.

sides.party_line_note: All 15 sponsors and cosponsors were Democrats; the bill never reached a floor vote, and Republicans controlled the Senate and its Energy Committee in 1995.

industries.note: The bill would close off new federal leases in waters adjacent to moratorium states, cutting into the industry's future drilling territory. Its interest in keeping those waters open runs against coastal residents' desire to keep drilling away from their shores.
New federal leases next to their states could bring drilling platforms, seismic surveys, and spill risk close to fishing grounds and beaches; the bill would block that.
